\section[o telefone]{o telefone — a phone}

\label{lesson:PT-C53-telefone}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for a pencil, then the Portuguese for a bag.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: o telefone}
\textbf{o telefone} — \textquotedblleft{}a phone\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{telefone} — borrowed, probably from French \emph{téléphone}. The French word was coined from Greek \emph{tēle}, \textquotedblleft{}far\textquotedblright{}, and \emph{phōnē}, \textquotedblleft{}voice\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB 2.1).
\end{cousinweb}

\end{grammarlens}

\section[o guarda-chuva]{o guarda-chuva — an umbrella}

\label{lesson:PT-C53-guarda-chuva}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for a bag, then the Portuguese for a phone.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: o guarda-chuva}
\textbf{o guarda-chuva} — \textquotedblleft{}an umbrella\textquotedblright{}. Literally \textquotedblleft{}guard-rain\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{guarda-chuva} is built from \textquotedblleft{}guard\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}rain\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB 2.1): a rain guard. The guard verb goes back to Frankish \emph{wardōn}, \textquotedblleft{}to keep, to guard\textquotedblright{}; the rain word $\leftarrow$ Latin \emph{pluvia} (EtymDB 2.1).
\end{cousinweb}

\section[o dinheiro]{o dinheiro — money}

\label{lesson:PT-C53-dinheiro}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for a phone, then the Portuguese for an umbrella.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: o dinheiro}
\textbf{o dinheiro} — \textquotedblleft{}money\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{dinheiro} $\leftarrow$ Latin \emph{denarius}, \textquotedblleft{}a Roman silver coin\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB 2.1) — inherited. Old Portuguese \emph{dĩeiro} lost the \emph{-n-} and kept it as a nasal vowel.
\end{cousinweb}

\textbf{o presente} — \textquotedblleft{}a present, a gift\textquotedblright{}.
